title: The Emperor's Dream of the Lost Teeth (ZH)
summary: An astrologer tells Akbar that all his relatives will die before him, causing royal fury. Birbal interprets the same prophecy with tact, winning praise. [ZH]
full_text:
One night, Emperor Akbar had a vivid and disturbing nightmare: he dreamed that all his teeth fell out of his mouth one by one, until only his gums remained.

Waking in cold sweat, Akbar summoned the court astrologer and asked for an interpretation.

The astrologer, a blunt and tactless man, looked at the astrological charts, gasped, and announced with gloomy certainty: 'Alas, Your Majesty! This is a terrible omen! The dream means that every single one of your relatives—your children, brothers, nephews, and cousins—will die before your eyes, leaving you alone in old age!'

Akbar was horrified and enraged by the grim pronouncement: 'Insolent wretch! You dare prophesy the death of my entire family before my face? Throw him into the dungeon!'

Still troubled, Akbar summoned Birbal and recounted the nightmare.

Birbal listened with a calm, gentle smile, bowed low, and said in a joyful voice:

'Rejoice, Your Imperial Majesty! This is the most magnificent, auspicious dream a monarch could ever receive!'

Akbar leaned forward: 'Truly? What does it mean, Birbal?'

Birbal replied with melodic eloquence:

'Sire, the dream reveals that heaven has blessed you with extraordinary longevity! It means that Your Majesty will live to a glorious, ripe old age, outliving all your peers, blessed with health and long life beyond all your contemporaries to guide Hindustan into an era of golden peace!'

Akbar's heart filled with joy and relief. He smiled broadly and rewarded Birbal with a string of pearls.

Later, Birbal remarked to a courtier:

'Notice, friend: both the astrologer and I stated the exact same factual reality—that the Emperor would live longer than his relatives.

'Yet the astrologer focused on death and sorrow, while I focused on long life and blessing. Truth is like a precious diamond; if you throw it like a stone into a man's face, you break his teeth. But if you set it gently upon a velvet cushion, he treasures it forever.'
